item.title: Three young girls drowned in separate incidents at Wailoaloa Beach
item.description: Three children, aged 5, 7 and 8 years, have died in two separate drowning incidents at Wailoaloa Beach in Nadi yesterday. Police say the first incident involved two girls, aged 8 and 7, who were found floating in the water by bystanders.
item.content:encoded:
Three children, aged 5, 7 and 8 years, have died in two separate drowning incidents at Wailoaloa Beach in Nadi yesterday.

Police say the first incident involved two girls, aged 8 and 7, who were found floating in the water by bystanders.

The two girls had accompanied their mother to the beach for a picnic when the incident occurred.

In a separate incident at the same beach, a 5-year-old girl was found floating near the shoreline by bystanders.

Police say the child had accompanied her father for a picnic when the incident occurred.

Police say both incidents will be investigated for possible negligence.

The three deaths bring the country's national drowning toll to 50, compared with 31 during the same period last year.

Police say the loss of three young lives is a tragic reminder of the importance of closely supervising children at all times, particularly when they are near water.

They stress that drowning is preventable when proper safety precautions are followed and warn that even a moment of complacency can result in the loss of a life.

item.title: Ba woman worried about how long her family can cope with prolonged dry weather
item.description: Suki vendor Leena Devi of Bebai Kona in Ba is worried about how much longer her family can cope with the prolonged dry weather conditions as water shortages continue to affect their cattle farming and livelihood. Speaking to fijivillage News, Devi says her family is struggling with low water supply and currently relies on water stored in tanks as a backup.
item.content:encoded:
Suki vendor Leena Devi of Bebai Kona in Ba is worried about how much longer her family can cope with the prolonged dry weather conditions as water shortages continue to affect their cattle farming and livelihood.

Speaking to fijivillage News, Devi says her family is struggling with low water supply and currently relies on water stored in tanks as a backup.

She says the dry conditions have also made it difficult to find suitable grazing areas for their cattle, forcing them to travel long distances.

Devi says she walks about one mile every day to catch a bus to Ba Market, where she sells suki to earn a living.

She says the dry weather has also affected her suki business , with rising prices and pest problems adding to the challenges.

Devi says suki previously cost between $40 and $50 per kilogram, but prices have now increased to more than $100 per kilogram.

She adds that business is currently very slow, making it difficult to earn an income.

item.title: Women contribute towards clean water supply in Burerua and surrounding villages
item.description: Women in Burerua in Tailevu and surrounding villages have joined forces with Government to secure access to clean water, contributing one-third of the funding needed to establish a water system that is helping address previous water shortages and improve hygiene. Former Water Authority of Fiji staff member Vani Bera says the Prime Minister's Office provided two-thirds of the funding, while women f
item.content:encoded:
Women in Burerua in Tailevu and surrounding villages have joined forces with Government to secure access to clean water, contributing one-third of the funding needed to establish a water system that is helping address previous water shortages and improve hygiene.

Former Water Authority of Fiji staff member Vani Bera says the Prime Minister's Office provided two-thirds of the funding, while women from two villages raised the remaining one-third to ensure the old reservoir water system could operate smoothly.

Bera, who is originally from Nadogo in Macuata and now lives in Burerua, Sawakasa, says the improved water supply has made a significant difference, particularly for women who prepare and sell food in Korovou town.

She says residents previously relied on an old reservoir and traditional water sources established by their elders, which would often dry up during prolonged dry weather.

Bera says the water shortages made it difficult for families to access clean water and also affected women selling food, as they needed reliable supplies for food preparation and hygiene.

She says she eventually raised the issue directly with the Prime Minister, who agreed to support two-thirds of the cost of improving the water system, with the women agreeing to contribute the remaining amount.

Bera says Korovou, Burerua and Veinuqa are currently fortunate to have access to drinking and clean water through pipes connected to the Namau water source.

She says she has also spoken to the Water Authority CEO, who informed her that the Namau water catchment is currently flowing well.

item.title: Child receives precautionary HIV treatment after alleged needle incident in Suva
item.description: A child who reportedly suffered a needle injury in Suva last week is recovering at home after receiving precautionary medication to reduce the risk of HIV infection. The Ministry of Health and Medical Services confirms that the child was initially taken to a health centre in Suva before being referred to the Colonial War Memorial Hospital on the same day.
item.content:encoded:
A child who reportedly suffered a needle injury in Suva last week is recovering at home after receiving precautionary medication to reduce the risk of HIV infection.

The Ministry of Health and Medical Services confirms that the child was initially taken to a health centre in Suva before being referred to the Colonial War Memorial Hospital on the same day.

The Ministry says the child was assessed, treated and started on post-exposure prophylaxis, commonly known as PEP, as a precaution.

The child has since returned home and is receiving follow-up care.

The Ministry stresses that receiving PEP does not mean the child has HIV.

T he source of the needle is unknown, and there is no information confirming whether it carried any infection.

The Ministry explains that PEP is a 28-day course of medication used to help prevent HIV infection following possible exposure.

The treatment is most effective when started as soon as possible, ideally within a few hours and no later than 72 hours after exposure.

The Ministry says the risk of HIV transmission from a needle injury is low and can be reduced further with early medical treatment.

Needle injuries can also carry a risk of hepatitis B and hepatitis C.

The Ministry confirms that the matter has been reported to the Fiji Police Force, and says it will not comment on the circumstances of the alleged incident while investigations continue.

The Ministry is also urging members of the public not to share information that could identify the child, the family, their school or community.

Parents are being reminded to teach their children never to pick up or touch needles and syringes found in public places.

The Ministry is also encouraging children to walk in groups when out in public and immediately inform a trusted adult if they are injured or approached by a stranger.

Anyone who suffers a needle injury is advised to gently wash the affected area with soap and running water and seek medical attention immediately.

The Ministry says people should not squeeze, scrub or suck the wound.

Meanwhile, the Ministry is calling on the public to stop spreading rumours linking the alleged incident to people living with HIV.

The Ministry stresses that there is no information about the source of the needle or the health status of anyone allegedly involved.

The Ministry warns that such speculation creates fear and discrimination and could discourage people from seeking HIV testing and treatment.

HIV testing, treatment and PEP are available free of charge at Ministry health facilities, with testing and treatment provided confidentially.

item.title: Sigatoka farmer claims his three-acre pawpaw farm was deliberately set on fire
item.description: A Sigatoka farmer is appealing for help after his three-acre pawpaw farm was set on fire last Saturday, leaving him worried about how he will support his young family and recover from the losses. Mohit Kumar says he suffered losses estimated at between $5,000 and $6,000 following the fire.
item.content:encoded:
A Sigatoka farmer is appealing for help after his three-acre pawpaw farm was set on fire last Saturday, leaving him worried about how he will support his young family and recover from the losses.

Mohit Kumar says he suffered losses estimated at between $5,000 and $6,000 following the fire.

He says he has been in the farming business for 30 years, and this is the first time he has experienced an incident like this.

Insert: Kumar on his source of income 9th Nov

Speaking to fijivillage News, Kumar says he was alerted about the fire by a neighbour, but by the time he reached the farm, it was too late to control the blaze.

Kumar , who is renting the land, says he is particularly worried about supporting his young children, who are attending school.

He claims that a group of boys have been drinking alcohol on his farm f or the past two to three years and believes they may have started the fire while intoxicated.

Kumar says he is not blaming anyone directly, but found beer bottles and cans scattered around the farm after the fire.

He says the issue of people drinking on farms has been ongoing and had been reported previously.

Kumar is calling on Police to conduct regular patrols along Valley Road and surrounding farms, saying people often gather there to drink alcohol.

He is also appealing to the Government for assistance through subsidised seedlings or other support to help him re-establish his farm.

Kumar says rebuilding his livelihood will be particularly difficult amid the El Niño conditions.
